blocks.title: When Radio Becomes Software
blocks.subtitle: Digitise first, then let code do the rest

blocks.text:
A traditional radio is built for one job. Its filters, mixers and demodulator are fixed in hardware, so an FM receiver can never become a GPS receiver.

A software-defined radio moves those functions into code. The hardware only tunes and digitises a slice of spectrum. What the radio does with it is decided by a program, and can be changed in seconds.

blocks.heading: Sampling the spectrum
blocks.text: The front end shifts a chosen band of radio frequencies down to baseband and an analogue-to-digital converter samples it. Each sample has two parts, **in-phase (I)** and **quadrature (Q)**, which together record both amplitude and phase. From that stream, software can filter, demodulate and decode any signal that fits inside the sampled bandwidth.

steps.text: **Tune.** A mixer and local oscillator shift the band of interest to a low frequency.
**Digitise.** A converter samples the signal as I/Q pairs at a rate at least equal to the bandwidth wanted.
**Process.** Software or an FPGA filters, shifts and demodulates the samples to recover audio, images or data.
**Reconfigure.** Loading a different program turns the same hardware into a different radio.

blocks.heading: Seeing the spectrum
blocks.text: Because an SDR captures a whole band at once, it can display it. A fast Fourier transform turns the samples into a spectrum, and stacking successive spectra forms a **waterfall** in which every transmitter appears as a trace. Engineers use this to find interference, study unknown signals and check that their own transmitters behave.

blocks.heading: Limits and responsibilities
blocks.text: Converters and front ends bound what software can do: dynamic range, noise and spurious signals all matter, and wide bandwidths produce data faster than a computer may be able to process. Receiving is generally permitted, but transmitting requires a licence or a licence-exempt band and equipment that stays within the rules. Check national regulations before transmitting.

blocks.question: Why does an SDR record I and Q instead of a single value per sample?
options: To capture both amplitude and phase of the signal
blocks.explanation: With both components, software can tell positive from negative frequencies and demodulate any scheme.

blocks.question: What mainly determines the widest signal an SDR can capture at once?
blocks.explanation: For complex sampling, the captured bandwidth is about equal to the sample rate.

blocks.heading: Key terms and next steps
blocks.text:
**Baseband**: a signal centred on zero frequency. **FFT**: fast Fourier transform. **Decimation**: lowering the sample rate after filtering. **Dynamic range**: the span between the weakest and strongest signals handled together. **Transceiver**: a device that both transmits and receives.
